claim: Build the entire low-poly blockout of a hard-surface object first -- every primitive, boolean, inset, and proportion decision -- with zero bevels and zero fine detail, and only start adding bevels once the full blockout silhouette is settled. Most beginners' 'big issue' is jumping into beveling/detailing before they have a basic shape to begin with.
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript, 2026-08-15): 'once you have the block out, that's when you can start adding your bevels... most people, they jump straight into that before they even have a basic shape to begin with, and that's a big issue.'
rejected_alternative: Adding bevels to individual primitives/features as each one is created, before the overall blockout's proportions and silhouette are confirmed against reference.
reason: Independently confirms this project's own already-adopted reasoning process for Level 5 ('reference -> ... -> primitive/blockout -> extrusion -> multi-view checking -> Subdivision', which implicitly defers finishing touches) and the extrude-then-subdivide order captured from the Blender Stack Exchange source earlier the same day -- a third source converging on the same blockout-first sequencing, now for bevels specifically rather than just subdivision.

claim: WHERE bevels are placed on a blockout -- which specific edges, not just how many or how large -- fundamentally changes the resulting silhouette and 'flow' of the object; the same base blockout can read as a completely different design depending on bevel edge selection, described as more consequential to the final look than almost any other single decision in hard-surface modeling ('the single most important thing in my opinion in hard surface modeling besides like general visual design').
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript): 'depending on where you place those bevels, you're going to completely change the shape of the model... Bevels are the single most important thing in my opinion in hard surface modeling besides like general visual design right because they make your models look you know significantly more interesting.' Demonstrated by beveling the same blockout at different edge combinations and comparing the resulting silhouettes live.
rejected_alternative: Treating bevel placement as a uniform finishing pass applied evenly to every edge, rather than a deliberate per-edge design decision with its own silhouette consequences.
reason: A judgment-level principle (not a mechanical procedure) directly relevant to this project's own standing bevel-weight policy: WHICH edges get bevel weight isn't just a sharp/round classification question, it's also a silhouette-design question that deserves the same deliberate attention as blockout proportions.

claim: Bevel size (width) directly controls perceived edge hardness independent of segment count: a large bevel reads as soft/rounded, a tiny bevel reads as hard/sharp while still being technically beveled -- giving continuous control over how 'defined' a given edge looks, tunable per edge on the same object for compositional variety.
supporting_evidence: Read directly (transcript): 'notice if the bevel is big it's a lot softer if the bevel is tiny it's really a lot harder on that edge and you can define the shapes a lot more... interesting so to speak.'
rejected_alternative: Using a single uniform bevel width across an entire object for consistency, rather than varying width per edge as a deliberate softness/hardness design choice.
reason: Directly relevant to this project's standing bevel-weight policy and the same-day open question about Bevel-before-vs-after-Subdivision: this adds a design dimension (varying bevel WIDTH per edge, not just presence/absence) that the current policy doesn't yet address.
